protocol_content.name: CARE Trial: Combined Autophagy inhibition and Radiation therapy to improve Efficacy in Canine Glioma
protocol_content.tagline: A research study evaluating a novel drug alongside radiation therapy for dogs with brain tumors.
protocol_content.description:
Dogs diagnosed with glioma, an aggressive brain tumor, often experience limited benefit from standard treatments such as radiation therapy alone. This clinical trial is evaluating a novel investigational drug called bisaminoquinoline-13 (BAQ-13) that may help improve how brain tumors respond to radiation therapy.


BAQ-13 works by blocking a process called autophagy, which cancer cells use to survive treatment. This study will evaluate whether BAQ-13 can safely reach brain tumors, be tolerated by dogs receiving radiation therapy, and show early signs of effectiveness.
protocol_content.requirements: An initial screening and eligibility workup, including physical and neurologic examination, blood work, and diagnostic imagingAdvanced brain imaging (MRI and CT scans) performed under general anesthesiaMinimally invasive brain tumor biopsies performed at enrollment and after treatmentIntravenous administration of an investigational drug (BAQ-13) twice weekly for 4 weeksConcurrent radiation therapy (standard of care)Blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sample collection at specified time pointsOvernight hospitalization following biopsy proceduresFollow-up visits, including in-hospital evaluations and telemedicine check-insCompletion of owner questionnaires to monitor quality of life and treatment effectsEnd of Study: When your family is ready to elect humane euthanasia, your dog will return to UC Davis. A brief examination will be performed prior to humane euthanasia. Following your dog’s death, a brain MRI will be performed, and they will undergo a routine necropsy. We will evaluate distribution of the drug in the brain, brain tumor, and vital organs (heart, lung, kidneys, liver). If your dog passes away or is euthanized elsewhere, the study team will arrange return to UC Davis for post-mortem evaluation.
protocol_content.responsibilities: If you choose to enroll your dog in this study, you will be responsible for:Covering the cost of initial diagnostic tests required to determine eligibility Bringing your dog to all scheduled hospital visits, treatments, imaging appointments, and follow-up evaluationsProviding complete and accurate medical history and records as requested by the study teamCompleting quality-of-life questionnaires and participating in scheduled check-ins (including telemedicine visits)Monitoring your dog at home and promptly reporting any health changes or concerns to the study teamFollowing all study-related instructions, including medication schedules and post-procedure careCommunicating with the study team if you are unable to attend a visit or if you are considering withdrawing from the studyParticipation is voluntary, and you may withdraw your dog from the study at any time.
protocol_content.whoCan: Dogs may be eligible if they:Have a suspected high-grade glioma diagnosed by brain MRIAre planned to receive conventional radiation therapyAre otherwise healthy enough for anesthesia and repeated hospital visits
protocol_content.benefits: Potential Benefits:It is possible that this therapy may provide a benefit to your dog. Studies in mice with gliomas have demonstrated an increase in survival time after this treatment, but it is unknown whether dogs will have the same benefit. While we cannot predict if your dog will live longer with this therapy, information obtained from your dog's participation in this trial will be critical to further develop this treatment, which has the potential to lead to a breakthrough in treatment for both dogs and humans with this deadly disease.  Potential Risks:All medical procedures carry risks, and experimental treatments have the potential for increased risks because they have not been used routinely. There are two factors of this trial that carry potential risk to your dog : 1) this trial is testing a novel drug that has not been administered to pet dogs before and 2) your dog will undergo two (2) brain biopsies over the trial period. If there are complications associated with the clinical trial, the study will cover up to $3000 in medical care costs provided by the UC Davis VMTH to address complications.Novel drug therapy: Any animal or human may have an idiosyncratic (“personal”) adverse reaction to the experimental drug used in this trial. Based on the use of this treatment in healthy dogs, we believe that the risk of serious adverse effects is small. However, this study may affect your dog in ways that are unknown. These may be a minor inconvenience or may be so severe as to cause death.Brain tumor biopsy: General anesthesia is required for brain tumor biopsy, which carries inherent risk to your dog. All patients undergoing general anesthesia at the UC Davis VMC are extensively evaluated and carefully monitored during each procedure to ensure their health and safety. The biopsy procedure itself entails making a small hole in the skull and collecting 2-3 samples of tumor using a large needle. Risks associated with this procedure are low (<10% occurrence), but can include bleeding, infection, neurological decline, or even death.
protocol_content.compensation:
Study covers:
Study-related MRIs and CT scans (excluding initial diagnostic MRI)
Brain tumor biopsies
Investigational drug and monitoring
Hospitalization related to study procedures
The study will provide $4,000 in financial support towards your dog’s radiation treatment costs at the completion of RT and BAQ-13 therapy.
protocol_content.timeCommitment:
Active treatment period: ~6 weeks

Follow-up monitoring: ongoing, including telemedicine and periodic hospital visits
